passage: Lalremsiami tucked her hair back and smiled. "Deepika, you asked why I stayed in the village after college when everyone went to Aizawl. Here's the thing. When I came back, there were no books for the kids. None. So I started a library in the church hall with forty books from my own shelf. Three years now. We have eight hundred books, and a small reading club every Friday. Last month, a girl who used to hide behind her mother read a whole story to the little ones. Afterwards she came up and said, 'I want to be a writer.' I went home and just sat on the steps for a long time. I'm not rich. I'll probably never be. But when I lock that hall door every evening, I feel like I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be."

qa.q: How many books did Lalremsiami start the library with?
qa.a: Forty books from her own shelf.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami mean when she says she feels exactly where she's supposed to be?
qa.a: She feels fulfilled and at peace in her work with the children, finding it more meaningful than wealth.

qa.q: What helped Lalremsiami's small idea grow over three years?
qa.a: Starting with what she had and keeping at it steadily, adding books and a regular reading club.

qa.q: How might the girl who wants to be a writer see the library?
qa.a: As a place that gave her courage and a dream she might not have found otherwise.

grounding: A young woman describes the deep sense of purpose she finds in a long-term community project.

passage: I'm Arnab, and I studied engineering with Irfan. Everyone assumed he'd go abroad. Instead he joined the district roads department. Two years ago I visited his posting. He took me to a village that used to get cut off every monsoon because the only road turned to mud. Pregnant women had to be carried out on cots. Irfan had spent eighteen months fighting paperwork and sitting with contractors to build an all-weather road. When we drove on it, an old woman waved at our jeep and shouted something. Irfan smiled but didn't say much. Later, over tea, I asked if he regretted not going abroad. He looked out at the fields for a while and said, "Not today." I think that meant something deep for him. I'm not sure I'll ever know exactly what.

qa.q: What happened to the village's only road every monsoon?
qa.a: It turned to mud and cut the village off.

qa.q: What might Irfan's quiet smile and 'Not today' suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He seems to feel a deep, quiet fulfilment from seeing the road help people, though he doesn't put it into many words.

qa.q: What helped Irfan finish the road?
qa.a: His persistence over eighteen months with paperwork and contractors, focused on a clear community goal.

qa.q: How might the old woman who waved feel about the new road?
qa.a: She likely feels grateful and relieved that her village is no longer cut off in the rains.

grounding: A friend describes a young engineer's quiet sense of purpose in work that serves a community.

passage:
Spring: Lalit, twenty-five, joined a legal aid clinic in the city after law school, earning far less than his classmates. His first weeks were paperwork and long queues of people with land disputes. He often wondered if he'd made a mistake.

Autumn: He took on the case of Farida, a widow whose husband's family had taken her small plot. Months of hearings. Missing documents. He found an old record in the district office basement, covered in dust.

The next spring: The court ruled in Farida's favour. Outside, she pressed both his hands and said, "My children will have a home." Lalit walked back to the clinic slowly, through the noisy market, and didn't notice the noise. That night, for the first time, he wrote down his five-year plan: stay, and train others to do the same.

qa.q: Where did Lalit find the old record?
qa.a: In the district office basement.

qa.q: How had Lalit's feelings about his job changed by the final spring?
qa.a: He went from doubting his choice to feeling deeply fulfilled, enough to plan his future around the work.

qa.q: What small step shows Lalit is turning fulfilment into a long-term goal?
qa.a: Writing down a five-year plan to stay and train others at the clinic.

qa.q: How might Farida's children be affected by the court's ruling?
qa.a: They now have a secure home, which may give them stability for years to come.

grounding: Shows over time a young lawyer finding a deep sense of purpose in work for community justice.

passage:
"Hafsa, you asked why I still teach the night school after all these years," Rukmini Didi said, stirring her tea on the office steps. "Let me tell you about the first time I felt it.

"I was twenty-four. Twelve women in a tin-roofed room, learning to sign their names instead of pressing a thumb. It was slow. Some nights only four came. I was tired, and my friends were getting promotions.

"Then one evening Sundari came in waving a bank slip. She had opened an account, alone, and signed it herself. She stood there with tears in her eyes, and I felt something settle in me, like a stone reaching the bottom of a well. Not happiness exactly. Rightness.

"That feeling doesn't come every day, beta. But once it comes, you know what you're for."

qa.q: How old was Rukmini Didi when she first taught at the night school?
qa.a: She was twenty-four.

qa.q: What did Rukmini Didi mean by feeling 'rightness' rather than happiness?
qa.a: She felt deeply settled, sensing that her work mattered and fitted who she was, which went beyond a passing good mood.

qa.q: What could Hafsa take from this story for Hafsa's own work?
qa.a: Hafsa could notice which moments bring that settled sense of purpose and let them guide long-term choices, even when progress is slow.

qa.q: How might Sundari have experienced that evening with the bank slip?
qa.a: She likely felt proud and independent, maybe for the first time, and wanted to share it with the teacher who helped her.

grounding: An elder recalls her first deep sense of purpose from community work in her mid-twenties.

passage:
The power went out ten minutes into Simran's Saturday science club, and the town's generator was still broken from the floods. Thirty kids sat in the dim community hall, restless. Her projector was useless.

"Didi, are we going home?" one boy asked.

Simran looked at the rain streaking the windows and had an idea. "No. Today we're studying water." They lined up bottles on the sill, measured the rain every half hour, and argued about why the river had risen so fast.

Vaibhav, who helped her, whispered, "You've been doing this every weekend for two years for free. Don't you get tired?"

"Of course," she said. Then a girl ran up holding a bottle. "Didi, it's gone up two centimetres!" Simran felt the tiredness fall away. She wanted these kids to be the engineers who fixed this town one day.

qa.q: How long had Simran been running the science club for free?
qa.a: For two years, every weekend, according to Vaibhav.

qa.q: What does Simran's tiredness falling away suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests the club gives her a deep sense of purpose tied to the town's future, strong enough to outweigh her exhaustion.

qa.q: How did Simran handle the power cut well?
qa.a: She turned the problem into the lesson by measuring rain, keeping the children engaged instead of cancelling.

qa.q: How might the children see Simran?
qa.a: They probably see her as someone who shows up no matter what, and her energy makes them excited about science.

grounding: Shows a young woman feeling deep purpose from long-term community work despite a power cut after floods.
